--- title: "Why Are Hospital Bills So Insanely Expensive?" subtitle: "The same hip replacement costs $29,000 in the U.S. and $7,700 in Germany. Here's where the money goes." author: "SixtyEight95" date: "2026-11-15" categories: [health care, cost of living, hospitals] image: infographic.png --- ::: {.cell} ::: A night in the hospital can cost more than a used car. A routine birth can come with a bill in the thousands, even with insurance. Everyone knows American hospital care is expensive. We wanted to know **how** expensive, compared with what, and **why.** ## The short answer ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} Hospital prices have grown about **17.3×** since 1980, while pay grew 4.7×. A hip replacement that private insurers paid **$29,006** for in the U.S. cost **$7,681** in Germany. The biggest reasons: private insurers pay hospitals about **254% of what Medicare pays**, hospitals have merged into local near-monopolies, about a quarter of hospital spending goes to administration, and hospital "list prices" are inflated far beyond cost. ::: ## 45 years of hospital prices, in hours of work Like our other cost-of-living stories, we measured hospital prices against what the average worker earns. If a hospital service took 100 hours of work to pay for in 1980, here's how many hours the same service has taken since. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Hospital care now takes about **3.7 times** as many hours of work as it did in 1980. Unlike college tuition, which has started getting easier to afford, hospital prices have stayed near their peak. ## The same procedure, around the world The International Federation of Health Plans compared what private insurers paid for the same hospital procedures in nine countries in 2022. These are actual payments, not list prices. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Hover over any dot to see the country. The U.S. is the most expensive for every procedure. The biggest gap of all is heart bypass surgery: **$89,094** in the U.S., versus **$16,936** in Germany and **$15,183** in Spain. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Median price paid by private insurers, 2022. Source: iFHP/HCCI 2024 report. |Procedure | U.S.| UK| Germany| Australia| Spain| |:----------------|-------:|-------:|-------:|---------:|-------:| |Heart bypass | $89,094| $25,804| $16,936| $17,741| $15,183| |Hip replacement | $29,006| $14,849| $7,681| $14,986| $6,780| |Knee replacement | $26,340| $15,216| $8,522| $13,609| $6,600| |C-section | $13,601| $8,910| $2,419| $7,742| $2,807| |Appendectomy | $13,560| $3,950| $3,980| $4,268| $2,622| |Vaginal birth | $8,655| $3,002| $1,361| $5,318| $2,175| ::: ::: ## Why: the four big reasons ### 1. Private insurance pays hospitals more than double what Medicare pays The same hospital, the same procedure, very different prices depending on who's paying. RAND studied claims from employer health plans across the country and found that in 2022, they paid hospitals **254% of what Medicare would have paid** for the same care. In some states it was over 300%. Medicare sets its prices. Private insurers have to negotiate them, and often they don't have much leverage, which leads to reason two. ### 2. Hospitals have merged into local near-monopolies Over the past few decades, hospitals have bought each other up. KFF found that in **47% of U.S. metro areas**, the entire hospital market is controlled by just one or two health systems. When an insurer has to include a hospital system in its network because there's no alternative, that system can charge more. Research consistently finds that hospital mergers raise prices, without clear improvements in quality. ### 3. A quarter of the budget goes to paperwork Billing in the U.S. is complicated: hundreds of insurers, each with its own rules, codes, and approval processes. One study found that administration took about **25%** of U.S. hospital budgets, about twice the share in Canada or Scotland. (The study's authors support a single-payer system, but the gap they measured is large under any interpretation.) ### 4. The "list price" is mostly fiction Every hospital has a "chargemaster," a master list of prices. These list prices bear little resemblance to what care costs. A study of Medicare cost data found the average hospital listed **$4.32** for every $1 of its actual costs, and up to about 28 times cost for CT scans. Medicare and insurers rarely pay list prices. The people who often get billed them are the **uninsured** and patients treated **out of network**, the ones with the least power to negotiate. ## The human cost About **20 million adults** owe significant medical debt (over $250), totaling at least **$220 billion**, according to KFF. Hospital bills are a big part of that. ## The fine print - **Different years.** Country prices and the Medicare comparison are from 2022, the administrative cost study is from 2011 data, and the list price study from 2013. The patterns have held up in later research, but the exact numbers have moved. - **Country prices are medians** of what private insurers paid, converted to U.S. dollars by the report's authors. Public systems in some countries may pay less. - **"Hours of work"** uses the government's hospital services price index and the average worker's hourly pay before taxes. It tracks how prices changed, not any one bill. - **What you personally pay** depends on your insurance, deductible, and whether the hospital is in network. ## The bottom line Health economists have been saying it for decades: American health care is expensive mainly because the **prices** are higher, not because Americans get far more care. For hospitals, private insurers pay far more than Medicare, merged hospital systems have the leverage to keep it that way, billing complexity adds a heavy layer of cost, and inflated list prices land hardest on the people least able to pay. --- **How we did this.** Procedure prices are from the International Federation of Health Plans and Health Care Cost Institute's *International Healthcare Cost Comparison Report 2024* (2022 data), read from the report's charts. The Medicare comparison is from RAND's hospital price transparency study (Round 5.1). Market concentration is from KFF. Administrative costs are from Himmelstein et al., *Health Affairs* (2014). List price markups are from Bai & Anderson, *Health Affairs* (2016). Medical debt is from KFF's analysis of Census survey data. The hours-of-work trend uses the CPI for hospital services (BLS series CUUR0000SEMD) and average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory employees, both via [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/).
